gm.name: United Kingdom
gm.road_lines: Yellow Outside - White Inside / White Outside - White Inside

items.html:
UK front plates are white, while back plates are yellow. Some plates have a blue strip on the left, but most do not.

Additionally, you might see a plate with a green ‘Zero Emissions’ strip.

NOTE: Ireland uses white front and back plates, always with a blue strip on the left.

The UK drives on the left side of the road.

NOTE: The UK, Ireland, Malta and Cyprus are the only European countries that drive on the left.

Double yellow road lines are often found on the sides of marked roads, especially in urban areas. These lines indicate a no stopping zone.

NOTE: These lines can also be found in Ireland.
These middle lines, that consist of long dashes with cat’s eyes (reflectors) in the gaps between the dashes, are a good clue for the UK.

The most common bollard in the UK looks like this. It has a rounded shape, with a red reflector on the front and a white one on the back. The base and top are black, with a white stripe in the middle.

The UK uses wooden poles. Pole steps bolted on the side of the pole are very common. These pole steps are shaped like a series of thin horizontal metal rods.

NOTE: Ireland also commonly uses wooden poles with pole steps.

Poles in the UK occasionally have a metal crossbar near the top with two diagonal supports forming a triangle shape.

NOTE: Ireland, as well as Sweden and Finland also use similar crossbars on some poles.

Chevrons are black with white arrows.

NOTE: Irish chevrons are black with yellow arrows. French chevrons are blue with white arrows.

Like most European countries, the UK uses triangular warning signs with a red border and a white background.

NOTE: This is mostly useful to distinguish between the UK and Ireland, as Ireland uses diamond-shaped yellow warning signs (being the only European country to do so).

Direction signs in the United Kingdom can be blue, green, or white. Look for the letters A or M, as these are the major roads in the country. Smaller roads start with B.

NOTE: Irish direction signs are typically bilingual, with Irish names in italics, making them easy to distinguish from the UK ones.

The UK commonly uses these white street signs with black text, that are positioned low to the ground. They are usually supported by two small posts. Many street signs in suburban areas will have a small cul-de-sac icon.

They can sometimes have different colours or feature small designs, like coats of arms.

UK yield signs feature the phrase “GIVE WAY”.

NOTE: Irish yields signs just have the word “YIELD”.

The yellow warning stickers on utility poles can be a good way to distinguish between the UK and Ireland.

The most important difference is that UK stickers feature a guy getting zapped by a lightning bolt.

The Irish stickers usually have a lightning bolt, but lack the guy getting zapped. They also often have an extra second rectangular sticker with a black outline, below the lightning bolt.
This yellow traffic bollard is commonly found in the UK.

Pedestrian crossing signs are almost non-existent in the UK. Instead, pedestrian crossings will often have these distinctive black and white striped poles, with a yellow light bulb on top.

NOTE: These signposts are also common in Ireland.

Rural metal gates with square corners are very common in the UK.

NOTE: This is mainly useful to distinguish it from Ireland, where similar gates typically have rounded corners. Gates in Northern Ireland also typically have rounded corners.

The British countryside tends to be very green, with lots of hedgerows lining the road. Low, rolling hills are common throughout most of the country.

NOTE: The Irish countryside looks very similar, so make sure to look at other clues before guessing.

Terraced houses (row houses) are very common in the UK. This housing type shares walls on both sides with neighbouring homes. You will also see a lot of semi-detached houses, which share just one side wall with another house.

NOTE: 61% of the population lives in terraced or semi-detached houses, significantly more than most other European countries. The only European countries where terraced houses are this common are Ireland and the Netherlands.

Red brick buildings are common in many parts of the UK.

NOTE: Red brick architecture is also common in the Netherlands, Belgium, and Denmark, as well as parts of northern France.

Suburbs in UK towns tend to have a recognizable look. They typically feature near-identical houses, often semi-detached, usually with well-manicured lawns. The road layout can be maze-like, with lots of cul-de-sacs and curvy roads.
Many British buildings have distinct-looking chimneys with multiple so-called chimney pots. These pots are usually round and brick-coloured.

Some buildings, both old and new, feature black-and-white timber framing.

NOTE: This is less common in Ireland.

The UK has Generation 4 “smallcam” coverage, which is mounted lower than regular Generation 4 and has a relatively big circular blur with a small protrusion at the front. The blur can also be fully transparent, making it harder to spot.
Occasionally, you can find one of the 4 country flags, which will tell you where in the UK you are.

A- and B-roads are grouped by their first digit, for example A380 and B3217 are located in the southwest of the country. Motorways also generally follow this pattern.

Beware that roads starting with any digit from 1 to 8 can also be found in Northern Ireland.

Landline phone numbers in the UK always have nine or ten digits after the 0 trunk code. The first two to four digits after the 0 are the area code. Unfortunately for Geoguessr players, there is not much rhyme or reason to their geographic ordering.

However, the area codes of some large cities are still worth memorising. The most important ones are summarised in this infographic. Notably, all of Northern Ireland uses the phone code 028, and all of London uses 020.

A complete overview of all other area codes is available in this infographic.
Bins in urban areas often have the city name on them.

The Scottish Highlands can be distinguished by the semi-barren, very mountainous landscape.

NOTE: A lot of Generation 4 coverage in the Highlands is from (early) spring, meaning that the vegetation often looks brown and yellow.

In addition, some of the most mountainous parts of Wales and Northern England can look similar.

In Scotland, you can often find these red and white bollards. They are round, bulky, and have a red-and-grey reflector that wraps all the way around.

They are sometimes found in other parts of the UK.

NOTE: The bollard looks similar to the French one. However, there are some small differences. For example, the Scottish bollard is round on the top, while the French one is more spiked.
These diamond-shaped ‘Passing Place’ signs are most commonly found in Scotland.

Welsh is a Celtic language that is spoken throughout Wales. Road signs in Wales are usually bilingual English and Welsh. Towns often have Welsh names too.

Welsh uses the letters D, W, and Y much more commonly than English. The double LL is also very distinct.

NOTE: Scottish Gaelic and Irish are both also Celtic languages. They can look somewhat similar to Welsh.

In Wales, markings on the road are in both English and Welsh. One of the best examples of this is ‘Araf’, which means ‘Slow’. This marking is only found in Wales.

NOTE: Araf is not the only Welsh language marking you can find, it is just the most common. Whenever you see an obviously non-English marking next to an English one, consider guessing in Wales.

Scottish Gaelic is a Celtic language that is closely related to Irish. They have a very similar look and use accent marks commonly. Common and recognizable letter clusters include bh, dh, fh, mh, ai, ea, eo, and ui.

Scottish Gaelic on road signs is found most commonly in the Scottish Highlands, and is almost always found north of Glasgow.

NOTE: Scottish Gaelic on road signs will often be in green or yellow text. This will not happen with Welsh or Irish on road signs.

It is common to see houses made of large blocks of sandstone or granite in Scotland. Granite buildings are common in Aberdeen, red sandstone is common in Glasgow and Dumfries, and yellow sandstone is common in Edinburgh.
Cornish palms (_Cordyline australis_) in the UK are most commonly found in the far southwest along the coast and in Jersey. Although, they can rarely be found all along the west coast up to Scotland.
These black stickers with yellow text sometimes appear on lampposts in Northern Ireland.
Warning stickers wrapped all the way around the utility pole are specific to Northern Ireland.

The Isle of Man is an island in the Irish Sea between the United Kingdom and Ireland. There is only Generation 2 coverage on the island. For country streak purposes, it is counted as part of the United Kingdom.

Plonk It has a more in-depth guide to the Isle of Man here.

Jersey is an island in the English Channel between France and England. There is only Generation 2 coverage on the island. For country streak purposes, it is counted as part of the United Kingdom.

Plonk It has a more in-depth guide to Jersey here.

Gibraltar is a British Overseas Territory located at the southern tip of the Iberian Peninsula, bordering Spain. For country streak purposes, the territory is counted as part of the United Kingdom.

Plonk It has a more in-depth guide to Gibraltar here.

Bermuda is a British Overseas Territory located in the North Atlantic Ocean.

Plonk It has a more in-depth guide to Bermuda here.

The Falkland Islands is a British Overseas Territory located in the South Atlantic Ocean.

Plonk It has a more in-depth guide to the Falkland Islands here.

South Georgia and the South Sandwich Islands is a British Overseas Territory located in the South Atlantic Ocean.

Plonk It has a more in-depth guide to the territory here.

The Pitcairn Islands is a British Overseas Territory located in the South Pacific Ocean.

Plonk It has a more in-depth guide to the Pitcairn Islands here.

The British Indian Ocean Territory is a British Overseas Territory, unsurprisingly located in the Indian Ocean.

Plonk It has a more in-depth guide to the British Indian Ocean Territory here.
The Lake District is very hilly, with a lot of exposed rocks and stone walls. It can look like the Scottish Highlands, but Scotland is generally less rocky.
London street signs have a distinct look. They usually feature the street name in black, followed by the postcode and borough in red.

Street name signs in Aberdeen and Aberdeenshire typically feature a simple blue background with white lettering.

NOTE: Central Aberdeen uses a different, black-and-yellow design.

Signs with green text underneath the street name, indicating the townland, can be found in the western part of Northern Ireland.

Especially towards the north of the shaded area, there may be a metal divider between the two lines.
Most street signs in the Wakefield council are black with a white outline and letters. They use the Monotype Rockwell Nova font.

Some of the Generation 4 coverage in London was taken by a white electric vehicle, with this distinct back of the car visible.

NOTE: A similar car was used in Dublin and Germany, so make sure to check out other clues as well.
The majority of poles and signposts in Birmingham have either yellow tape or yellow paint wrapped around them. Lampposts will also usually have this yellow sticker.
Speed signs with green borders with the text “Twenty’s Plenty” are mostly found in and around Glasgow.

steps.title: Maps and resources
steps.html:
GeoGuessr’s own official maps are not very good, for a variety of reasons. Plonk It recommends you play these maps instead:

  • AI Generated United Kingdom (map link) - 110k+ locations, not pinpointable.
  • IntersectionGuessr - United Kingdom (map link) - 80k+ locations, mostly pinpointable.

In addition, here are some resources to help you practise the UK:

  • Plonk It United Kingdom (map link) - This map contains locations for practising each meta in the Plonk It United Kingdom guide from step 2 to 3.

lm.name: A1 Roads
lm.note:
The main A-roads in the UK are grouped by their first digit after the A, for example A380 will be located in the southwest of the country.

Beware that A-roads starting with any digit from 1 to 8 can also be found in Northern Ireland.

Tip: Imagine the UK as a clock, the digits go clockwise, starting at 1 and ending at 9.

lm.name: Aberdeenshire + Aberdeen street sign
lm.note: This street sign is unique to Aberdeenshire and Aberdeen. Its blue with white capitalized text and does not have any border around it.

lm.name: Bedford sticker
lm.note: This unique sticker with the black eagle logo on top is found in Bedford and areas around it.

lm.name: Belfast mountains
lm.note:
Depending where you are in Belfast, you can often see these distinct mountains/hills with lots of trees on it (gets more bald on the top) to the west/north-west, sometimes with 1 or 2 towers on top of it. Hills can also be seen in the east/south east.

If your not sure these mountains are the Belfast mountains, check for clues to confirm your in Northern Ireland and it will 100% be Belfast.

lm.name: Bin - City name
lm.note: Bins in urban areas often have the city name on them.

lm.name: Birmingham - phone code 0121
lm.note:
Landline phone numbers in the UK always have nine or ten digits after the 0 trunk code. The first two to four digits after the 0 are the area code. Unfortunately for Geoguessr players, there is not much rhyme or reason to their geographic ordering.

However, the area codes of some large cities are still worth memorising. The most important ones are summarised in this infographic. Notably, all of Northern Ireland uses the phone code 028, and all of London uses 020.

lm.name: Birmingham yellow tape/paint
lm.note: The majority of poles and signposts in Birmingham have either yellow tape or yellow paint wrapped around them. Lampposts will also usually have this yellow sticker.

lm.name: Blue stickers
lm.note:
Blue stickers/stickers with blue in them (excluding blue letters/numbers) are found in North Wales.

If you want, you can learn which blue stickers are found in which region:

  • Light blue stickers are found in Anglesey.
  • Green white dark blue stickers are found in Denbighshire.
  • Purple white light blue stickers are found in Conwy.
  • Generic blue stickers are found in Flintshire, Wrexham and Gwynedd, they are very rare in Gwynedd and are mostly found in Flintshire and Wrexham (east part of North Wales).

Other blue stickers can also be occasionally seen in North Wales.

lm.name: Boat trekker
lm.note: Boat trekkers are limited to three locations: the River Thames, which runs through London, Keyhaven Lake, and Loch Ness lake. Each have different boats and very different landscapes.

lm.name: Bristol street sign
lm.note: Street signs in Bristol will always have ''BS'' with a number written on the right side. This one is easy to remember because BS stands for Bri-Stol.

lm.name: Cambridgeshire + Coventry + Derby + South Tyneside sticker
lm.note:
This white sticker with black letters and numbers and a diamond with small text under it is found in Cambridgeshire, Coventry, Derby and South Tyneside.

Cambridgeshire + Coventry have 6 or less letters/numbers and white space between the text and diamond.

Derby always has 7 letters/numbers and no space between the text and diamond.

South Tyneside always has a blue sticker under it.

NOTE: This excludes Peterborough which has its own sticker, which always has ''PCC" written on a white sticker.

lm.name: Cardiff - phone number 029
lm.note:
Landline phone numbers in the UK always have nine or ten digits after the 0 trunk code. The first two to four digits after the 0 are the area code. Unfortunately for Geoguessr players, there is not much rhyme or reason to their geographic ordering.

However, the area codes of some large cities are still worth memorising. The most important ones are summarised in this infographic. Notably, all of Northern Ireland uses the phone code 028, and all of London uses 020.

lm.name: Castle stone walls
lm.note: Stone walls that look like a castle wall are mostly found in North Wales. Especially towards Anglesey and in Anglesey. They can also sometimes be found elsewhere in Wales.

lm.name: Ceredigion sticker
lm.note: This yellow sticker, sometimes white, with 3 numbers and 4 numbers under it can be found in Ceredigion. What makes it extra distinct, is that its pasted on another white sticker behind it.

lm.name: Cornish palms
lm.note: Cornish palms (Cordyline australis) in the UK are most commonly found in the far southwest along the coast and in Jersey. Although, they can rarely be found all along the west coast up to Scotland.

lm.name: Cornwall plate
lm.note: This very distinctive black plate with a letter followed by 3 numbers is commonly found in Cornwall. The letter and numbers are always either white or yellow, sometimes mixed together.

lm.name: Cumbria architecture
lm.note:
In Cumbria, especially around Keswick often has these white houses with black ladder-like frames on the corners, often with black frames around the windows.

NOTE: These frames can be found elsewhere

lm.name: Cylindrical hay bales
lm.note: Cylindrical hay bales laying around on these hilly agricultural fields can mostly be found in the region north of Aberdeen. They can very rarely be seen elsewhere in Scotland.

lm.name: Dark red bricks architecture
lm.note:
North West England around Manchester/Lancashire has a lot of dark red bricks. Dark brown, black and white doors are common, aswell as black and white lintels around windows are often seen.

NOTE: Dark red bricks can be found elsewhere too.

lm.name: Distinct stone walls
lm.note:
Houses and walls that are made out of pebble stones or flint stones with red brick build in to them are found in East Anglia, most commonly in Norfolk, they can also be found on the south of Sussex and East Sussex.

These stones can rarely have a different color like yellow or black.

lm.name: Edinburgh - phone number 131
lm.note:
Landline phone numbers in the UK always have nine or ten digits after the 0 trunk code. The first two to four digits after the 0 are the area code. Unfortunately for Geoguessr players, there is not much rhyme or reason to their geographic ordering.

However, the area codes of some large cities are still worth memorising. The most important ones are summarised in this infographic. Notably, all of Northern Ireland uses the phone code 028, and all of London uses 020.

lm.name: Fife Sticker
lm.note: This white sticker with 2 black numbers and 3 pieces of small text, 1 above the number and 2 under it, can be found in Fife.

lm.name: Flat Fens landscape
lm.note: Eastern England tends to be more flat. The Fens area of reclaimed land has very distinct "Dutch-like" landscape. Its typically very flat and open, with straight roads and small dikes, often hedgerows absent. The area around the town Goole also features a similar landscape.

lm.name: Flat landscape with big hedgerows
lm.note:
It is very common to see big hedgerows in north eastern Anglia, combined with its very flat landscape, most likely will be around that area.

NOTE: Its also common to see just normal hedgerows in this region, having normal hedgrows with flat landscape is still a good clue for this region.

lm.name: Glasgow - phone number 0141
lm.note:
Landline phone numbers in the UK always have nine or ten digits after the 0 trunk code. The first two to four digits after the 0 are the area code. Unfortunately for Geoguessr players, there is not much rhyme or reason to their geographic ordering.

However, the area codes of some large cities are still worth memorising. The most important ones are summarised in this infographic. Notably, all of Northern Ireland uses the phone code 028, and all of London uses 020.

lm.name: Glasgow pink sticker
lm.note: This pink sticker with the text ''PEOPLE MAKE GLASGOW'' can be found on these trash bins in Glasgow.

lm.name: Glasgow street sign
lm.note: Glasgow street signs are white with a black frame in it.

lm.name: Gravel front gardens
lm.note: Lincolnshire, Norfolk and the Fens commonly have bungalows with neat gravel front gardens.

lm.name: Greater London bus stop sign
lm.note: This bus stop sign is found in Greater London. It has a very distinct logo on the top half.

lm.name: Greater Manchester bus stop sign
lm.note:
This busstop sign can be found in Greater Manchester, it has the phone code on it and the M logo on the top left corner with a bunch of other things like a bee on the right. The logo's and phone code can only be seen on one side.

NOTE: A different version can be seen in older coverage, which will be completely white with a huge M logo on it.

lm.name: Hampshire and West Sussex sticker
lm.note: This white sticker with 1 - 2 numbers and lots of small text with a logo under it is found in Hampshire and West Sussex. Sometimes there is also text and a logo above the number, or there is only text without a number.

lm.name: Hebrides Islands
lm.note: The areas around the Hebrides Islands often have a rocky, treeless tundra-like landscape, but is by far mostly seen in the Western Isles.

lm.name: Industrial buildings
lm.note: Urban areas in the Midlands, especially around the Black Country and Birmingham, often have a very industrial appearance. This region is well known for its history of heavy industry, with factories, warehouses, and old brick buildings.

lm.name: Isle of Man - Gen 2 cam
lm.note:
Coverage on the Isle of Man is limited to Generation 2.

This camera can be recognized by the lower camera quality and circular blur above and below. Colours will also seem slightly off.

lm.name: Isle of Man - Isle of Man licence plate
lm.note: Similar to the United Kingdom, the Isle of Man uses white front licence plates with yellow rears, but with a red strip on the left.

lm.name: Isle of Man - Striped kerbs
lm.note: Striped kerbs can sometimes be seen along main roads.

lm.name: Kielder Forest
lm.note: The Kielder Forest and some areas around it is filled with dense pine trees. While pine trees can be seen in other places as well, no other region has them in the same abundance as the Kielder Forest.

lm.name: Lake District
lm.note: The Lake District is very hilly, with a lot of exposed rocks and stone walls. It can look like the Scottish Highlands, but Scotland is generally less rocky.

lm.name: Leeds - phone number 0113
lm.note:
Landline phone numbers in the UK always have nine or ten digits after the 0 trunk code. The first two to four digits after the 0 are the area code. Unfortunately for Geoguessr players, there is not much rhyme or reason to their geographic ordering.

However, the area codes of some large cities are still worth memorising. The most important ones are summarised in this infographic. Notably, all of Northern Ireland uses the phone code 028, and all of London uses 020.

lm.name: Leeds District street sign
lm.note: Street signs in Leeds District will always have ''LS'' with a number written on the right side. This one is easy to remember because LS stands for Leed-S.

lm.name: Leicestershire pole plate
lm.note:
This black plate with 1 - 3 numbers, useally yellow, is found in Leicestershire. They look like Northern Ireland stickers but those are flat instead of a plate and have no supports around the pole.

NOTE: For some odd reason, they very rarely appear in Leicester itself.

lm.name: Limestone architecture
lm.note: This golden colored Limestone is very common in and around Cotswold, especially towards the north.

lm.name: Lincolnshire sticker
lm.note:
Yellow stickers with ''LCC'' (which stands for ''Lincolnshire County Council'') written under the numbers can be found in Lincolnshire. ''LCC" can sometimes be hard to see, if you only see ''CC" clearly, that also confirms your in Lincolnshire.

NOTE: This doesn’t apply to North Lincolnshire and North East Lincolnshire (Scunthorpe, Grimsby and surrounding areas) which are separate councils.

lm.name: Liverpool - phone number 0151
lm.note:

However, the area codes of some large cities are still worth memorising. The most important ones are summarised in this infographic. Notably, all of Northern Ireland uses the phone code 028, and all of London uses 020.

lm.name: Liverpool street signs
lm.note: Liverpool street signs often an L on the bottom right corner, standing for Liverpool, towards the centre in the city you will get signs with a unique shape and often have the text ''City of Liverpool'' written on them.

lm.name: London - Gen 4 white electric vehicle
lm.note:
Some of the Generation 4 coverage in London and surrounding areas was taken by a white electric vehicle, with this distinct back of the car visible.

NOTE: A similar car was used in Dublin and Germany, so make sure to check out other clues as well.

However, the area codes of some large cities are still worth memorising. The most important ones are summarised in this infographic. Notably, all of Northern Ireland uses the phone code 028, and all of London uses 020.

lm.name: London street signs
lm.note: London street signs have a distinct look. They usually feature the street name in black, followed by the postcode and borough in red.

lm.name: Manchester - phone number 161
lm.note:
Landline phone numbers in the UK always have nine or ten digits after the 0 trunk code. The first two to four digits after the 0 are the area code. Unfortunately for Geoguessr players, there is not much rhyme or reason to their geographic ordering.

However, the area codes of some large cities are still worth memorising. The most important ones are summarised in this infographic. Notably, all of Northern Ireland uses the phone code 028, and all of London uses 020.

lm.name: Mansions
lm.note: Wealthy areas in the UK are often in the Home Counties near London, especially Surrey and Berkshire, where you’ll find big houses and gated mansions along leafy roads.

lm.name: New Forest landscape
lm.note: The New Forest has a distinctive look, with a mix of forest and heathland landscape.

lm.name: Newcastle architecture
lm.note: In urban areas around Newcastle, it’s common to see red brick walls extending from houses to enclose gardens. These walls often include garage doors built into them.

lm.name: North York Moors
lm.note: North York Moors has a distinct moorland landscape. Features rolling, mostly brown moorlands, with rough grasses and patches of low vegetation

lm.name: Northern Ireland - Black sticker with yellow text
lm.note:
These black stickers with yellow text sometimes appear on lampposts in Northern Ireland.

NOTE: Wiltshire have the same stickers on lamposts, so be aware of that.

lm.name: Northern Ireland - phone number 028
lm.note:
Landline phone numbers in the UK always have nine or ten digits after the 0 trunk code. The first two to four digits after the 0 are the area code. Unfortunately for Geoguessr players, there is not much rhyme or reason to their geographic ordering.

However, the area codes of some large cities are still worth memorising. The most important ones are summarised in this infographic. Notably, all of Northern Ireland uses the phone code 028, and all of London uses 020.

lm.name: Northern Ireland - Rounded edge gate
lm.note: Gates in Northern Ireland have these rounded edges, unlike mainland UK which have square edges.

lm.name: Northern Ireland warning sticker
lm.note: Warning stickers in Northern Ireland are almost always fully wrapped around the pole. Unlike mainland UK, which commonly uses just 1 or 2 stickers on the pole.

lm.name: Orange tape
lm.note: In Northamptonshire, you can often find orange tape wrapped around poles. A white sticker with blue text and numbers and a diamond shaped icon on it can commonly be seen aswell on the poles.

lm.name: Orkney Islands
lm.note: The Orkney islands is mostly treeless and open, with vast farmland in many places and mostly small hills.

lm.name: Pennines architecture
lm.note: Pennines areas of Yorkshire and Lancashire often have this very distinctive dark gritstone with patches of black on the bricks. Their also more common towards the south.

lm.name: Perth and Kinross sticker
lm.note: This white sticker with a black letter and 4 numbers, and has "FAULT'' with a phone number written under it is found in Perth and Kinross. Most of the times, it has a small frame in the sticker around the text.

lm.name: QR code sticker
lm.note: This distinctive yellow sticker features a 6 number code followed by a QR code. This is a great clue that you are in the counties north of London. As it has consistently only been found in the following counties: Norfolk, Suffolk, Essex, Cambridgeshire, Bedfordshire, Hertfordshire and Buckinghamshire. It is frequently found on rural wooden electricity poles.

lm.name: Red roofs
lm.note: Eastern UK can have these very distinct red clay pantile roofs, especially on older houses. This is commonly found on the eastern half of the coast from Fife down to East Anglia.

lm.name: Scotland - Houses made of large blocks of sandstone or granite
lm.note: It is common to see houses made of large blocks of sandstone or granite in Scotland. Granite buildings are common in Aberdeen, red sandstone is common in Glasgow and Dumfries, and yellow sandstone is common in Edinburgh.

lm.name: Scotland - Passing place sign
lm.note: These ‘Passing Place’ signs are 95% found in Scotland. Wales has Welsh written under it and the England version is the same.

lm.name: Scotland - Red and white bollards
lm.note:
In Scotland, you can often find these red and white bollards. They are round, bulky, and have a red-and-grey reflector that wraps all the way around.

They are sometimes found in other parts of the UK.

NOTE: The bollard looks similar to the French one. However, there are some small differences. For example, the Scottish bollard is round on the top, while the French one is more spiked.

lm.name: Scotland - Scottish Gaelic
lm.note:
Scottish Gaelic is a Celtic language that is closely related to Irish. They have a very similar look and use accent marks commonly. Common and recognizable letter clusters include bh, dh, fh, mh, ai, ea, eo, and ui.

Scottish Gaelic on road signs is found most commonly in the Scottish Highlands, and is almost always found north of Glasgow.

NOTE: Scottish Gaelic on road signs will often be in green or yellow text. This will not happen with Welsh or Irish on road signs.

lm.name: Scottish Highlands
lm.note:
The Scottish Highlands can be distinguished by the semi-barren, very mountainous landscape.

NOTE: A lot of Generation 4 coverage in the Highlands is from (early) spring, meaning that the vegetation often looks brown and yellow.

In addition, some of the most mountainous parts of Wales and Northern England can look similar.

lm.name: Scottish Highlands - Northern region
lm.note: Within the Scottish Highlands, the northern part of it is much less mountainous than the rest of the highlands. It has mostly just hills, with sometimes a few or less mountains visible in the distance.

lm.name: Seagull
lm.note: This is Gulliver the Seagull. If you see him, you will be in Colwyn Bay.

lm.name: Sheffield - phone number 0114
lm.note:
Landline phone numbers in the UK always have nine or ten digits after the 0 trunk code. The first two to four digits after the 0 are the area code. Unfortunately for Geoguessr players, there is not much rhyme or reason to their geographic ordering.

However, the area codes of some large cities are still worth memorising. The most important ones are summarised in this infographic. Notably, all of Northern Ireland uses the phone code 028, and all of London uses 020.

lm.name: Shetland Islands
lm.note: You can recognize the Shetland Islands by the very low amount of vegetation and useally no trees at all. Patches of trees can rarely be seen on these islands. You will never see mountains either, its all just hills with mostly grass and some small bushes. Some parts also look like the Faroe Islands.

lm.name: Snowdonia
lm.note:
Some roads, mostly in the south and north Snowdonia, have these distinct dark grey stone walls with vertical stones on top of it along the road. The landscape itself is very forested and mountainous, but less forested in the north east.

NOTE: These stone walls can be found elsewhere too, most commonly in North Wales.

lm.name: South east Northern Ireland region
lm.note: This small region all the way south of ''mourne area of outstanding natural beauty'' features slightly hilly landscape with lots of rockwalls and distinct mountains to the north, further west there will be hedgerows instead of rockwalls but the same mountains can still be seen.

lm.name: South West England architecture
lm.note:
South West England, especially Cornwall and Devon, features a lot of stone and light pastel buildings. These materials are sometimes mixed together so they feature both materials in one building.

NOTE: Wales can sometimes look similar so check for other clues (if available) to confirm your in South West England.

lm.name: Southampton street sign
lm.note: Street signs in Southampton almost always have the text ''City of Southampton'' written on them. This meta is super easy to know because it literally just says the city name on it and these signs can be find everywhere in the city.

lm.name: Southern Wales valley architecture
lm.note:
This valley north-west of Cardiff has a very recognizable look. Featuring many terraced houses and brown stone walls with colorful windows and often have this unique shape made out of pastel around the windows and doors. The towns are build on hills so its always hilly.

NOTE: Similar valleys with the same look can be find elsewhere in Wales but this one is by far the biggest.

lm.name: Stone walls
lm.note:
The Lake District, North Pennines, Yorkshire Dales, Nidderdale and Peak District are very hilly and have alot of stone walls. Stone walls can appear in other national parks and places but not as much as these 5 national parks, which have the majority of stone walls.

The Lake District is by far the hilliest, with plenty of exposed rock. Along with the North Pennines and Yorkshire Dales, it sometimes features abandoned-looking barns. Beyond that, I’m not sure how to tell them apart.

lm.name: Suffolk sticker
lm.note: This white sticker with blue numbers and letters and commonly a phone number under it can be found in Suffolk.

lm.name: T shape sticker
lm.note: A white sticker with numbers forming a T shape, can be found in Pembrokeshire and Carmarthenshire.

lm.name: Thatched roofs
lm.note: Thatched roofs are the most common in the middle of southern England, especially around Hampshire and Wiltshire.

lm.name: Tudor architecture
lm.note: Tudor architecture, mostly black and white, sometimes with red bricks mixed are mostly found in West Midlands and East Anglia. They can also be found in Wales, mostly towards the England border. They can also be quite common in the south like Kent and Sussex and sometimes parts of Surrey and Oxfordshire. They can very rarely be found in Northern England and almost never in Scotland.

lm.name: Twenty’s Plenty speed signs
lm.note: Speed signs with green borders with the text “Twenty’s Plenty” are mostly found in and around Glasgow.

lm.name: Wales - ARAF road marking
lm.note:
In Wales, markings on the road are in both English and Welsh. One of the best examples of this is ‘Araf’, which means ‘Slow’. This marking is only found in Wales.

NOTE: Araf is not the only Welsh language marking you can find, it is just the most common. Whenever you see an obviously non-English marking next to an English one, consider guessing in Wales.

lm.name: Wales - Roadline gap
lm.note: Gaps in roadlines are most commonly found in Wales.

lm.name: Wales - Welsh language
lm.note:
Welsh is a Celtic language that is spoken throughout Wales. Road signs in Wales are usually bilingual English and Welsh. Towns often have Welsh names too. Welsh uses the letters D, W, and Y much more commonly than English. The double LL is also very distinct.

NOTE: Scottish Gaelic and Irish are both also Celtic languages. They can look somewhat similar to Welsh.

lm.name: Wales architecture
lm.note:
Many Welsh towns have a mix of stone and pastel buildings, often with colorfull paint around doors and windows. This is especially common in the western parts near the coast.

NOTE: South West England can sometimes look similar so check for other clues (if available) to confirm your in Wales.

lm.name: Wales sheep
lm.note: Sheep are most common in Wales, but can be found elsewhere too. So if you see a bunch of sheep and its very hilly/mountainous with typical Wale-ish landscape, with many hedgerows and green grassy fields and you have no other clues, you might aswell guess Wales.

lm.name: Weald Hanging tiles
lm.note: Weald Hanging tiles are the most common in Sussex and Kent. But can sometimes be found elsewhere in the southern half of England.

lm.name: West Midlands County bus stop sign
lm.note: This bus stop sign is found in West Midlands County. It has a very distinct logo on the top half.

lm.name: West Northern Ireland - Green text
lm.note:
Signs with green text underneath the street name, indicating the townland, can be found in the western part of Northern Ireland.

Especially towards the north of the shaded area, there may be a metal divider between the two lines.

lm.name: A-Type w/o reflectors
lm.note:
UK only use A-Type guardrails which makes it useful to differentiate between Ireland and the UK.

NOTE: Ireland uses both A & B-Type.

lm.name: UK license plates
lm.note: In the UK, license plates are white on the front and yellow on the back. In Ireland, both the front and back plates are white.

lm.name: UK road lines
lm.note:
These middle lines, that consist of long dashes with cat’s eyes (reflectors) in the gaps between the dashes, are a good clue for the UK.

Note: You can find it rarely in Ireland.

lm.name: English
lm.note: English is the main language of the United Kingdom (I bet you knew that already). Keep in mind that English is also spoken in Ireland, aswell as Malta and Gibraltar within Europe. It is not uncommon to find English in other countries aswell, where is acts as an international language.

lm.name: Scottish Gaelic
lm.note:
Scottish Gaelic is a Celtic language closely related to Irish. They have a very similar look and use accent marks commonly. Common and recognizable letter clusters include bh, dh, fh, mh, ai, ea, eo, and ui.

Scottish Gaelic on road signs is found most commonly in the Scottish Highlands, and is almost always found north of Glasgow.

NOTE: Scottish Gaelic on road signs will often be in green or yellow text. This will not happen with Welsh or Irish on road signs.

lm.name: Welsh
lm.note:
Welsh is a Celtic language spoken throughout Wales. Road signs in Wales are usually bilingual English and Welsh. Towns often have Welsh names too.

Welsh uses the letters D, W, and Y much more commonly than English. The double LL is also very distinct.

In Wales, markings on the road are in both English and Welsh. One of the best examples of this is Araf, which means Slow. This marking is only found in Wales.

NOTE: Scottish Gaelic and Irish are both also Celtic languages. They can look somewhat similar to Welsh.

lm.name: Northern Ireland bus stop signs
lm.note: In Northern Ireland, most bus stops will have light blue UlsterBus signs.

lm.name: Scottish passing place signs
lm.note: These ‘Passing Place’ signs are unique to Scotland.

lm.name: Roadlines
lm.note:
• Double yellow road lines are often found on the sides of marked roads, especially in urban areas.
  • These lines indicate a no stopping zone.

NOTE: These lines can also be found in Ireland.

lm.name: flat pole top
lm.note: It is sometimes hard to distinguish France, Ireland, and the UK. An easy trick is to focus on the tops of the wooden poles: UK has a flat top

lm.name: pole steps
lm.note:
The UK uses wooden poles. Pole steps bolted on the side of the pole are very common. These pole steps are shaped like a series of thin horizontal metal rods.

NOTE: Ireland also commonly uses wooden poles with pole steps.

lm.name: Aberdeen architecture
lm.note: Aberdeen is a very easy recognizable city, 99% of all buildings are made out of grey sandstone.

lm.name: Belfast mountains
lm.note:
Depending where you are in Belfast, you can often see these mountains with lots of trees on it (gets more bald on the top) to the west/north-west, sometimes with 1 or 2 towers on top of it. Hills can also be seen in the east/south east.

If your not sure these mountains are the Belfast mountains, check for clues to confirm your in Northern Ireland and it will 100% be Belfast.

lm.name: Birmingham yellow tape/paint
lm.note: The majority of poles and signposts in Birmingham have either yellow tape or yellow paint wrapped around them. Lampposts will also usually have this yellow sticker.

lm.name: Bristol street sign
lm.note: Street signs in Bristol will always have ''BS'' with a number written on the right side. This one is easy to remember because BS stands for Bri-Stol.

lm.name: Edinburgh architecture
lm.note:
Edinburgh buildings are mostly made out of yellow/brown sandstone.

NOTE: Glasgow also has yellow/brown sandstone but also has red sandstone buildings.

lm.name: Glasgow pink sticker + architecture
lm.note: This pink sticker with the text ''PEOPLE MAKE GLASGOW'' can be found on these trash bins in Glasgow. The buildings in Glasgow are also made of red sandstone and yellow sandstone.

lm.name: Greater Manchester bus stop sign
lm.note:
This busstop sign can be found in Greater Manchester, it has the phone code on it and the M logo on the top left corner with a bunch of other things like a bee on the right. The logo's and phone code can only be seen on one side.

NOTE: A different version can be seen in older coverage, which will be completely white with a huge M logo on it.

lm.name: Leeds street sign
lm.note: Street signs in Leeds District will always have ''LS'' with a number written on the right side. This one is easy to remember because LS stands for Leed-S. The street sign in the top left is only found in the center.

lm.name: Liverpool street sign
lm.note: Liverpool street signs often an L on the bottom right corner, standing for Liverpool, towards the centre in the city you will get signs with a unique shape and often have the text ''City of Liverpool'' written on them.

lm.name: London street sign
lm.note: London street signs have a distinct look. They usually feature the street name in black, followed by the postcode and borough in red.

top.html:
UK front plates are white, while back plates are yellow. Some plates have a blue strip on the left, but most do not.

Additionally, you might see a plate with a green ‘Zero Emissions’ strip.

NOTE: Ireland uses white front and back plates, always with a blue strip on the left.
top.raw: UK front plates are **white**, while back plates are **yellow**. Some plates have a blue strip on the left, but most do not. Additionally, you might see a plate with a **green **[‘Zero Emissions’](/images/united-kingdom/UK_Zero_Emission_License_Plate.png) strip. NOTE: Ireland uses white front and back plates, always with a blue strip on the left.

top.html:
The UK drives on the left side of the road.

NOTE: The UK, Ireland, Malta and Cyprus are the only European countries that drive on the left.
top.raw: The UK drives on the **left side** of the road. NOTE: The UK, Ireland, Malta and Cyprus are the only European countries that drive on the left.

NOTE: These lines can also be found in Ireland.

top.html: The most common bollard in the UK looks like this. It has a rounded shape, with a red reflector on the front and a white one on the back. The base and top are black, with a white stripe in the middle.
top.raw: The most common **bollard** in the UK looks like this. It has a rounded shape, with a red reflector on the front and a white one on the back. The base and top are black, with a white stripe in the middle.

top.html:
The UK uses wooden poles. Pole steps bolted on the side of the pole are very common. These pole steps are shaped like a series of thin horizontal metal rods.

NOTE: Ireland also commonly uses wooden poles with pole steps.

top.html:
Poles in the UK occasionally have a metal crossbar near the top with two diagonal supports forming a triangle shape.

NOTE: Ireland, as well as Sweden and Finland also use similar crossbars on some poles.
top.raw: Poles in the UK occasionally have a **metal crossbar** near the top with two diagonal supports forming a triangle shape.  NOTE: Ireland, as well as Sweden and Finland also use similar crossbars on some poles.

top.html:
Chevrons are black with white arrows.

NOTE: Irish chevrons are black with yellow arrows. French chevrons are blue with white arrows.
top.raw: Chevrons are **black with white arrows**. NOTE: Irish chevrons are black with yellow arrows. French chevrons are blue with white arrows.

top.html:
Like most European countries, the UK uses triangular warning signs with a red border and a white background.

NOTE: This is mostly useful to distinguish between the UK and Ireland, as Ireland uses diamond-shaped yellow warning signs (being the only European country to do so).
top.raw: Like most European countries, the UK uses **triangular warning signs** with a red border and a white background. NOTE: This is mostly useful to distinguish between the UK and Ireland, as Ireland uses diamond-shaped yellow warning signs (being the only European country to do so).

top.html:
Direction signs in the United Kingdom can be blue, green, or white. Look for the letters A or M, as these are the major roads in the country. Smaller roads start with B.

NOTE: Irish direction signs are typically bilingual, with Irish names in italics, making them easy to distinguish from the UK ones.
top.raw: Direction signs in the United Kingdom can be **blue, green, or white.** Look for the letters **A** or **M**, as these are the major roads in the country. Smaller roads start with **B**. NOTE: Irish direction signs are typically bilingual, with Irish names in italics, making them easy to distinguish from the UK ones.

top.html:
The UK commonly uses these white street signs with black text, that are positioned low to the ground. They are usually supported by two small posts. Many street signs in suburban areas will have a small cul-de-sac icon.

They can sometimes have different colours or feature small designs, like coats of arms.

Many street signs in suburban areas will have a small cul-de-sac icon. They can sometimes have [different colours](https://goo.gl/maps/Uc9Wf1fjrpvfSTBM8) or feature small designs, like [coats of arms](https://goo.gl/maps/8Di7Wx8TC3dvs8gKA).

top.html:
UK yield signs feature the phrase “GIVE WAY”.

NOTE: Irish yields signs just have the word “YIELD”.
